1.pericope_label: The names of the sons of Israel; seventy souls; Joseph dies and the children of Israel multiply

schools.summary: Hold the divisions of the Pentateuch deliberate, the opening verses being a connecting link that proves the book was issued separately; compute the seventy and estimate how many more entered Egypt once wives, husbands and retainers are counted; take “household” in its eastern breadth; date the book’s span at three hundred and sixty years; and trace the words for the increase back to the blessings of creation and of the flood.

Infer from the opening conjunction that no division of the books had yet been made and the history ran on continuously; state that the small number going down is recorded to be compared with the number coming out; and set the whole increase against the appearance that the descent into Egypt had abolished the covenant.

Give both names of the book and the codex that calls it the departure from Egypt; date its span at a hundred and forty-five years; confine “household” to children and grandchildren; and explain the order of the names by the mothers.
Find in the number seventy the number of the nations among which the earth was divided, the bounds of the peoples having been set by the number of the children of Israel.

debates: Whether the book opens a distinct work or continues Genesis: Ellicott argues from the recapitulation that it was issued separately, Gill argues from the opening conjunction that no division existed.
How long a period the book covers — Keil says three hundred and sixty years and Clarke a hundred and forty-five, between the same two termini, neither noticing the other.
How wide “every man and his household” reaches — retainers and house-born servants included (Ellicott) or children and grandchildren only (Wesley).
What the number seventy is recorded for: to be compared with the multitude that left (Gill), because the reckoning is exact (Calvin), or because it matches the number of the nations (Henry).
outliers: Ellicott alone computes the seventy item by item and estimates the size of the party that actually entered Egypt.
Keil and Clarke alone date the book, and their figures differ by more than two centuries.
Calvin alone reads the descent into Egypt as an apparent abolition of the covenant which the increase refutes.
Wesley’s note on the number seventy reproduces Henry’s in order and wording, so the two are not independent here.

8.pericope_label: A new king who knew not Joseph; let us deal wisely with them; taskmasters and the treasure cities

schools.summary: Collect the older identifications of the king without choosing among them; explain the forgetting of Joseph by his own moderation in asking nothing for his people; hold that the exaction broke the terms on which the Israelites were admitted, and that the aim was affliction rather than revenue; and note that the verb for dealing wisely is oftener used well than ill.

Name a particular king and date him; make “knew not” a repudiation of Joseph’s system rather than ignorance of him; suspect a double burden of labour and tribute; and set out five distinct aims in the oppression, with the fear that it drew many into Egyptian worship.

Deny that the word “new” establishes a change of dynasty, whatever other grounds may; declare for a particular king on Egyptological grounds; refuse the reading that makes the address a public assembly; test the king’s claim against the populations and find it a deliberate exaggeration; and distinguish the two grades of officers in the Egyptian forced-labour system.
Turn the forgetting of Joseph into a warning that the place of our satisfaction may become the place of our affliction, and that those loved in one generation may be hated in the next.

debates: Who the new king was: one of four candidates canvassed by Gill, Clarke and Ellicott, against Keil’s denial that the word “new” settles even whether the dynasty changed.
What “knew not Joseph” means — ignorance and forgetting (Henry, Ellicott), deliberate repudiation of his policy (Clarke), or an ingratitude occasioned by Joseph’s own restraint (Calvin).
Whether the king addressed an assembly: Clarke and Calvin suppose a council of estates, Ellicott denies that any assembly is in view.
Whether the king’s claim about numbers was true — Ellicott alone tests it and calls it a lie.
What rank the taskmasters held: superintendents over the labour (Ellicott) or officers of tribute and taxation (Gill, Clarke).
outliers: Keil alone refuses the identification question on the ground that the adjective will not bear the weight put on it.
Ellicott alone computes the two populations and convicts the speaker of misrepresentation.
Calvin alone traces the forgetting of Joseph to a virtue in Joseph himself.
Wesley alone enumerates the several ends the oppression was meant to serve, and alone suspects it of producing apostasy.
Wesley’s note on the forgetting of Joseph reproduces Henry’s almost verbatim, the second such overlap in this chapter.

12.pericope_label: The more they were afflicted the more they multiplied; the Egyptians made their lives bitter with hard bondage

schools.summary: Deny that the increase under affliction was natural and refer it to providence; strengthen the rendering of the Egyptians’ vexation; document the character of Egyptian forced labour from the monuments and the historians; and answer the objection that the Egyptians did not build in brick.

Read the Hebrew as making the increase strictly proportional to the affliction, and extend the proportion beyond the case; note that the word for rigour is the one the later law forbids Israel to use toward a brother; set out the stages of the brickmaking; and generalise the paradox to the growth of the Church under persecution.

Describe the intended and the actual effect of the labour on the people’s strength, and compare the palm tree that grows under weight; read the verse as a contest between divine mercy and royal cruelty in which the design against the Church was frustrated; and observe that the failure hardened the oppressors instead of softening them.

debates: Why the people increased under oppression: a providence overruling nature (Ellicott), a strict proportion between suffering and growth (Clarke), a physical effect of labour on strength (Gill), or the frustration of a design against the Church (Calvin).
How far the paradox may be generalised — Wesley extends it to the whole history of the Church under persecution, Clarke extrapolates it to sufferings that never occurred.
What “with rigour” conveys: ferocity and oppression, in the very word the law later forbids to Israel (Clarke), or what breaks a man’s strength (Gill).
Whether the Egyptians built in brick at all — Ellicott raises the question and answers it from the monuments.
outliers: Clarke alone notices that the word describing Egypt’s cruelty is the word Israel is afterwards forbidden to deserve.
Ellicott alone brings monumental and historical evidence for the conditions of the labour and for the use of brick.
Calvin alone observes that the failure of the policy made the oppressors crueller rather than kinder.
Gill and Calvin both reach for the palm tree that grows under weight.

15.pericope_label: The king commands the midwives to kill the male children; but the midwives feared God

schools.summary: Weigh the case for Egyptian midwives and decide for Hebrew on the names and the wording; ground the refusal not merely in humanity but in the knowledge that the seed of Abraham was elect, distinguishing the fear of God from the dread of punishment; and rank the crime against every recorded instance of child-killing.

Show that the construction will bear either nationality and set out the arguments on both sides without deciding; reject the identification of the disputed word with the modern birth-chair and commend an emendation reading it as children; and note that the God the midwives feared is named as the personal and true one.

Take the midwives for Egyptians whom the Hebrews commonly employed, or else assume they were Hebrews who knew the ancient prohibition of bloodshed; make the two named women chiefs over many others; and report the rabbinic derivation of the disputed word from the word for children.
Ask why the grown men were not attacked instead of the infants, and answer from the depth of cruelty in the corrupt heart and the enmity against the seed of the woman.

debates: Whether the midwives were Hebrew or Egyptian: Gill argues both sides and decides for Hebrew, Wesley decides for Egyptian, Ellicott shows the grammar will bear either and leaves it open, while Clarke’s argument for their refusal silently assumes they were Hebrews.

What the disputed word in the sixteenth verse means — a stone trough, the modern birth-chair, or an emendation reading it as “children”; Clarke finds the last in the rabbis and Ellicott credits it to a modern scholar and calls it tempting.

Why the midwives refused: because God punishes wrongdoing (Ellicott), because his law forbids bloodshed (Gill, Clarke), because his wrath is worse than a king’s (Wesley), or because they knew the seed they were told to destroy was the elect seed (Calvin).
How many midwives were involved — two, or two chiefs over hundreds (Clarke, Wesley).
outliers: Calvin alone rests the refusal on the midwives’ knowledge of the election of Abraham’s seed rather than on humanity or law.
Calvin alone measures the command against the recorded instances of child-killing and finds it without parallel.
Ellicott alone declines to settle the nationality of the midwives after stating the case on both sides.
Henry alone asks why the persecution fell on infants rather than on the men.

18.pericope_label: Pharaoh questions the midwives; their answer, their reward, and the houses God made

schools.summary: Deny the king any motive but fear of rebellion; convict the midwives of lying and of sinning in it, rejecting both the rabbinic excuse and the category of the serviceable lie, while holding that God rewards his children’s stained works out of paternal indulgence; and refer the houses to the Israelites rather than the midwives on the masculine pronoun and the settled sense of the idiom.

Defend the answer as literally true — women inured to labour in the open air bear easily, as observation outside Scripture confirms — so that there was neither lie nor prevarication, and God was pleased with the midwives’ frankness; report Shuckford’s repunctuation making Pharaoh the builder of the houses; and take the easy births as the finger of God that emboldened the disobedience.

Grant that the answer was probably true but not the whole truth, a half truth taken as refuge by women who lacked the courage of their convictions, or else read it as a deception that simply succeeded; and insist with Augustine that what God rewarded was not the falsehood but the fear of God and the kindness shown, the houses being families given to the midwives themselves.

debates: Whether the midwives’ answer was true (Clarke, Wesley), a half truth (Ellicott), a successful deception (Keil), or a plain lie and a sin (Calvin), with Gill setting out both readings and choosing neither.
Whether God rewarded the midwives despite the lie (Keil quoting Augustine, Ellicott, Calvin) or because there was no lie to overlook (Clarke).
Who received the houses — the midwives (Keil, Wesley, Ellicott) or the Israelites (Calvin, and Clarke at the end) — and who built them, God or Pharaoh (Shuckford, reported by Clarke).
Whether the masculine pronoun settles the question, Calvin holding that it does and Clarke reporting that such forms are interchanged elsewhere.
outliers: Calvin alone holds that the midwives sinned, and builds from it a general doctrine that no action is free from stain and that God rewards works he would otherwise condemn.
Clarke alone argues the point from observation outside Scripture, including a labouring woman he saw delivered between one day’s work and the next.
Clarke alone reports Shuckford’s repunctuation, which makes Pharaoh rather than God the builder of the houses and turns the reward into a further measure of surveillance.
Ellicott alone remarks that nothing indicates the houses were Hebrew ones.

22.pericope_label: Pharaoh charges all his people to cast every Hebrew son into the river

schools.summary: Restrict the edict to Hebrew children on the authority of the Targums and the Septuagint, the wider order being ruinous to Egypt itself; and read the escalation as judgment on a reprobate given over to madness, with the daughters spared to breed slaves and extinguish the names, the whole then turned against the persecutions of the writer’s own century.

Take the river as chosen because it was sacred, the children being an offering meant at once to secure the inundation and to exterminate the race; date the edict between the births of Aaron and Moses and argue from the census numbers that it was soon revoked; and reproduce a patristic allegory of the chapter at length in order to condemn allegory as a method.

Call the Septuagint’s addition unnecessary; establish from Sparta, Athens, Rome, Syria, Carthage and Plato that such an edict is in no respect improbable; and raise against the river as the means the pollution of a god and the fouling of the only drinking water, before allowing that the children may have been offerings to the Nile or to its crocodile-headed god.

debates: Whether the Septuagint’s added words “to the Hebrews” are needed to limit the edict — Gill leans on them and on the Targums, Ellicott calls them unnecessary because the context already limits it.

Why the river was chosen: as a sacrifice to a sacred stream (Clarke, and Ellicott as a conjecture of last resort), against Ellicott’s own objections that corpses would pollute a god and foul the only drinking water.
Why the daughters were spared — Gill refers the reader back to his earlier note, while Calvin gives a calculation about slave-breeding and the extinction of the Hebrew names.
How long the edict stood, and whether the number of men at the exodus requires that it was revoked early (Clarke).
outliers: Clarke alone dates the edict and argues from the census figures that it must have been short-lived.
Clarke alone reproduces a patristic allegory of the whole chapter at length, and does it in order to reject allegorical exposition as a method that lets any passage mean anything.
Ellicott alone catalogues infanticide among the ancient nations to argue that the edict is historically credible.
Calvin alone treats the sparing of the daughters as a deliberate policy of slave-breeding and name-extinction, and alone applies the verse to the persecutions of his own day.
